# Magnetic deep eutectic solvents: formation and properties† Ruifen Shi,ª Fengyi Zhou,ª Yu Chen, ID *b Zhenghui Liu, ID *c Shuzi Liuª and Tiancheng Mu ID *a

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are well-known as novel solvents due to their unique properties, which are indispensable for the development of green chemistry in the future. CoCl2.6H2O and NiCl2.6H2O-based DESs, which could be called magnetic DESS (MDESs) for short in view of their responsive behavior to an external magnetic field, have been widely used in many industrial applications, such as biomass treatment, electrolytes, and material preparation. For better application and full-scale development of these MDESs in various fields, eleven MDESs were prepared in this work by using CoCl2.6H2O and NiCl2.6H2O as hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) with alcohols, carboxylic acids and amides as hydrogen bond donors (HBDs), respectively. The intermolecular interactions between the components of MDESs were characterized via FTIR, 1H NMR and DSC analysis. In addition, physicochemical properties including density, viscosity, conductivity, ionicity, pH values, surface tension, thermostability and solvatochromic parameters were investigated. All MDESs exhibit acid characteristics and have good conductivity comparable with ionic liquids (ILs) and other DESs used for electrolytes. The results show that stronger H-bonding networks in Ni-based MDESs make them have higher density, viscosity, polarity and surface tension values than Co-based MDESs. Moreover, all prepared MDESs possess a good conductivity behavior which could be comparable to that of common organic solvents and ILs. According to this work, we could better comprehend the behavior of Co/Ni-based MDESs and choose the appropriate one for particular applications.

## Introduction Green chemistry is a significant research branch of future chemical industry development, which caters to the idea of being environmentally friendly and sustainable.¹ Over 70% of chemical engineering processes involve solvents, most of which are organic solvents at present. As is known to us all, organic solvents are toxic, flammable and easily volatile in general, causing a negative influence on the human body and natural environment. Consequently, eco-friendly, less toxic and safe novel alternative solvents are extremely in demand. In recent years, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), as emerging green solvents, have attracted more attention given their excellent properties of low cost, easy preparation, negligible vapor pressure and so on,²⁻⁴ and they were first introduced by Abbot et al. in

On account of the designability and tunability of DESs, they have been applied in various applications, such as in extraction and separation,⁸,⁹ biomass treatment,¹⁰⁻¹² material preparation,¹³˒¹⁴ and so on.

In recent years, "Type II" DESs have received a lot of attention in the materials field. Hydrated metal halides are regarded as economically and technically promising components to form DESs for industrial processes.15 Specifically, Wang *et al*. have verified that the DES of FeCl3·6H2O:urea could act as a catholyte, which exhibits a good reversibility and higher battery capacity.16 A DES composed of FeCl3·6H2O and ethylene glycol has been reported to catalyze the conversion of cellulose, and it acts not only as a catalyst but a separation medium.17

Zn-based DESs have been prepared and used for PET degrada-tion reactions. 18 Moreover, the Ni/Co-based DESS were favored to be used as precursors to prepare catalyst and adsorbent materials in view of the special solvent environment. 19-21 Furthermore, they manifested a notable performance in gas separation based on the coordination ability of metal ions as well. 22,23 This type of DES typically includes a magnetic transi-tion metal, such as Fe(III), Co(Ⅱ), Ni(II), Mn(II) and Zn(Ⅱ), called magnetic DESS (MDESS) here. The physicochemical properties of MDESs are important to help us to understand their features and have a better application in various fields. 24,25 However, there are few studies on Co and Ni-based MDESs. Herein, eleven Co and Ni-based MDESS by using CoCl2.6H2O and NiCl2.6H2O act as HBA components, and alcohols, carboxylic acids and amides as HBD components were designed, prepared and characterized. Then, a comprehensive and systematic investigation on the properties and the intermolecular interac-tions between the components of the formed MDESs character-ized by FTIR, 1H NMR and DSC analysis were carried out. Temperature-dependent physicochemical properties such as density, viscosity and conductivity were performed at 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, and 75 °C. pH values, surface tension and solvato-chromic parameters were determined at room temperature. In addition, a Walden plot was applied to determine the ionicity. The results obtained would reveal the characteristics of these prepared MDESs as potential industrial solvents.

# Experimental ## Materials Cobalt(Ⅱ) chloride hexahydrate (CoCl2.6H2O, 98%), nickel(Ⅱ) chloride hexahydrate (NiCl2.6H2O, 98%), xylitol (Xyl, 98%), and acetamide (Ace, 99%) were all obtained from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Ethylene glycol (EG, 99%) was purchased from InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd (Beijing, China). L(+)-Lactic acid (LA, 90%) was acquired from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Glycerol (Gly, 99%) was bought from Beijing Tongguang Fine Chemical Co. LTD. Urea (99%) was supplied by Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Nile red and 4-nitroaniline were purchased from J&K Scientific Ltd. All chemicals were dried thoroughly before use.

Synthesis The Co and Ni-based MDESS were prepared according to the reported methods. 26 CoCl2.6H2O and NiCl2.6H2O were used as HBAs, and some typical polyols, amides and acids were chosen as HBDs (Fig. 1). The MDESs were obtained by mixing the HBA and HBD with a certain molar ratio (mainly 1:2 in this work) under heating (70 °C) and stirring (500 rpm). After a moment, a clear dark-blue or dark-green homogeneous liquid could be observed except for NiCl2.6H2O with xylitol. The obtained MDESS were dried under the vacuum environment at 80 °C for 24 h. ## Characterization The magnetic measurements were performed on a Model 7404 vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM, Lake Shore Corp, America). Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra were recorded on an FT-IR spectrometer (Tensor 27, Bruker) in the range of 4000 to 500 cm⁻¹. The nuclear magnetic resonance ¹H NMR spectra were recorded on a Bruker Avance 400 MHz spectrometer with D₆-dimethyl sulfoxide as the standard and the chemical shift data were later processed by the MestReNova Program. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was performed using a DSC Q200 (TA Instruments, USA) with a heating rate of 5 °C min⁻¹ under a nitrogen atmosphere. All the eutectic solvents were run in aluminum hermetic crucibles, which were cooled to -90 °C before heating up to 25 °C. TGA curves were measured by using a TGA Q4000 (PerkinElmer Instruments Inc.) in ramp mode (ramp 10 °C min⁻¹ to 400 °C, platinum pan). The density measurements were carried out using an Anton Paar DMA 5000 M density meter with the accuracy of ±5 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³. And the viscosities for MDESs were measured with an Anton Paar AMVn viscosity meter using a falling ball technique, and the repeatability of the viscosity is <0.1%. The ionic conductivity was measured using a conductivity instrument (DDS-307A, INESA). The pH values were measured by a pH-meter (PHS-3C, Shanghai INESA Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd, China). The surface tension of MDESS was measured using a tensiometer QBZY-1 (Wilhelmy platinum plate methods, Shanghai Fangrui Instrument Co., Ltd.) with the range of 0-600 mN m⁻¹ and the accuracy of ±0.1 mN m⁻¹. The density, viscosity, conductivity, pH and surface tension values of each MDES were measured three times, and the average values are reported. For the measurement of Kamlet-Taft parameters, Nile red (NR) and 4-nitroaniline (NA) were dissolved in methanol with a concentration of 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ and then dried under vacuum at 40 °C. Then 20 µL of the dye solutions was added to a quartz cuvette containing 2.0 mL of the prepared MDES. A UV-visible spectrophotometer (Cary 5.0, Varian) was used to obtain the λmax and duplicates of each MDES were measured at room temperature.

# Results and discussion ## Magnetic properties of MDESs The magnetic response behaviors of the prepared MDESs were investigated by vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 2a, all MDESs display a linear response, which indicates their paramagnetic behavior.27 From a magnetic susceptibility point of view, the Co-based MDESs have a higher strength than Ni-based MDESs in general. But a higher content of HBD will weaken the magnetic response significantly. Moreover, the provided photographs in Fig. 2b show the static microdroplets of MDES6 and MDES11 both began to move in the presence of a magnetic field. Other MDESs showed a similar magnetic response. Briefly, the prepared MDESs present magnetic behavior.

depicted in Fig. 3b. In the spectra of the formed MDES3 and MDES8, the O-H stretching vibration peaks are both wider than those of pure LA and the C=O absorption peaks shift to a lower wavenumber. The phenomena prove the formation of hydrogen bonds between metal hydrated salts and LA. In terms of acetamide, the N-H asymmetrical stretching, N-H symmetrical stretching, in-plane N-H bending, the N-H wagging bending and C=O stretching vibration are ascribed to peaks at 3375 cm⁻¹, 3190 cm⁻¹, 1625 cm⁻¹, 1149 cm⁻¹ and 1672 cm⁻¹, respectively. After the formation the MDESS, two sharp absorption peaks of N-H stretching vibrations in the range of 3540–3180 cm⁻¹ become smooth and approximate a broad peak on the whole. Meanwhile, the C=O stretching vibrations generate bathochromic shifts and the broad N-H wagging bending vibration peak disappears. Thus, the weakening or disappearance of N-H stretching vibration peaks as well as the red shifts confirm the existence of a hydrogen-bonding network in MDESS. Compared with urea, the two N-H stretching vibration peaks are weak and the in-plane N-H bending vibration peaks disappear for MDES6 and MDES11. Similarly, the results prove the formation of hydrogen bonds between urea and hydrated metal halides. In a word, the formation of MDESS is to be credited to the hydrogen-bonding interaction among components.

Proton nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR) is an effective technique to verify the HB interaction between components of DESs. In this work, the comparisons of chemical shifts of MDESS and related pure HBD components (solvent is D6- DMSO, 2.50 ppm) are presented in Fig. 3c and d. Hydrogen bonding is a vital factor to impact the chemical shift of protons. 28 For alcohols and acids, O-H is a typical group and the active hydrogen proton could be used to form a H-bond. As shown in Fig. 3c, pure EG has one peak at 4.55 pm corresponding to the OH group. After adding the CoCl2.6H2O or NiCl2.6H2O, the OH group in EG shifts to 4.38 ppm or 4.39 ppm. The chemical shift of the CH2 group shifts up-field and the shape has a change in MDES1 and MDES7. This variation can also be seen in the spectra of Xyl, Gly and LA- based MDESs. In amide-based MDESS, N-H as a polar group is prone to form hydrogen bonding. Compared with pure acetamide, the chemical shift of the NH group shifts up-field in MDES5 and MDES10. In contrast, the N-H in urea-based MDESS shifts downfield in comparison with the pure urea component (Fig. 3d). There might be a stronger interaction between hydrated metal halides and urea. To sum up, the hydrogen-bonding network exists in all MDESS.

To gain further insight, a differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) experiment was carried out to confirm the formation of MDESS. As shown in Table 2, all the prepared MDESS present a low glass transition temperature (T_g) which is below -35 °C. Moreover, there are just subtle differences in λmax between the MDESs composed with the same HBA. On the basis of the equations, solvatochromic data for the MDESS at room temperature are listed in Table 2. From the results, the HBD acidity parameter α of MDESS ranges from 0.91 to 1.20. In general, when the MDESs have the same HBA, the acidity increases in the order amides < polyols < acid, which is the same with the variation of π* values. The high acidic and polar nature might be caused by the carboxyl groups in the acid.35 In contrast, the β values of acid-based MDESs are the lowest among all MDESS. On the whole, the Ni-based MDESS have slightly higher solvatochromic parameter values than those of Co-based ones, indicating the HBA has a major regulatory effect. Moreover, these parameters were measured in the Ni: Gly system with a different molar ratio (shown in Table S2, ESI†) as well. The comparison results indicate that the increase of -OH groups will decrease the acidity and polarity, but the β values are mainly affected by HBA, which are consistent with previous reports.35 To better elucidate the solvation properties, a 3D plot was used to compare the prepared MDESs with typical organic solvents and ionic liquids (Fig. 4b). The results show that the α values of MDESs are close to those of methanol but superior to those of other selected solvents. Besides, all MDESs have higher β values as well. For the polarity, the MDESs could be comparable to the selected organic solvents and ionic liquids. Given the above, the MDESS have a fascinating solvation performance.

# Density Density is an essential and important physical property to understand the behavior of solvent. Meanwhile, it also influences the design and operation of processes in the environment and various industrial applications.37 Thus, it is crucial to identify the behavior of density with respect to temperature. In this study, the density of the MDESs was measured at different temperatures (25, 35, 45, 55, 65, and 75 °C), and the results are depicted in Fig. 5a. This is due to the increased activity and mobility of these MDESs following the heat boost, which are equal to increasing the molar volume of the solvent. Thus, the density of the MDES decreases with the increase of temperature. All the recorded density values of the prepared MDESs are below 1.60 g cm⁻³. The MDES11 has the highest density value (1.584 g cm⁻³) at 25 °C among these MDESs. This might be caused by a stronger intermolecular interaction between NiCl₂·6H₂O and urea. In particular, the density values of MDES11 and MDES6 both have a sharp declining tendency when urea acts as a HBD. On the contrary, the variation in other MDESs is nearly consistent. This illustrates that the urea-based MDESs have a more intensive thermal expansion, which causes poor stability in the heating process. The minimum density value belongs to MDES3 (1.335 g cm⁻³) at 25 °C, but this value is still higher than that of the majority of common organic solvents. ³⁸ Moreover, for the MDESs with the same HBD components, the density value of Ni-based MDES is always greater than that for Co-based MDESs, indicating that HBA plays a crucial factor in it. As expected, the viscosity of each MDES decreases with increasing temperature exponentially. This indicates that the viscosity values of MDESS are highly sensitive toward temperature compared with density. In particular, the viscosity decreases rapidly during the initial warming process, and then it gradually approaches a balance value at higher temperature. This variation of viscosity is consistent with the reports.42 It is noticeable that the viscosity of the studied MDES ranges from 84.3 to 10907.2 mPa s at 25 °C. Co:Xyl has the maximum viscosity value which is 6 to 100 orders of magnitude higher than that of the other MDESs. This could be attributed to the stronger hydrogen bonding network between CoCl2·6H2O and xylitol compared with other MDESS, which intensively influences the mobility of free species within MDES2. Generally, the sugar alcohol-based DESs possess a higher viscosity due to the existence of more robust 3D intermolecular hydrogen-bond networks.43 Moreover, with CoCl2·6H2O as a HBA and alcohols as a HBD, the viscosity values increase in the following order: MDES1 < MDES4 < MDES2. This result is consistent with a previous report that more hydroxyl groups in DESs result a higher viscosity.42 The extra hydroxyl groups promote a stronger hydrogen bonding interaction among components, which makes a viscous eutectic mixture. Moreover, this order indicates that the increase of chain lengths of the HBD further leads to the formation of a higher viscosity eutectic mixture. It could be explained in that higher molar mass side chains make DESs have stronger van der Waals forces, which results in insufficient mobility and high viscosity.44 Specially, MDES4 has a far higher viscosity value compared to MDES1. This might be related to the mole ratio of the eutectic components CoCl2·6H2O with glycerol (1:3). In the same way, the viscosity values of Ni-based MDESS with alcohols as HBD are in the following order: MDES9 > MDES7. As a result, the structures of HBDs are an important factor in determining viscosity of MDES. Among the prepared MDESS, the viscosity values of Ni-based MDESs are higher than those of the Co-based ones with the same HBD components. This result shows that there is a stronger hydrogen bonding interaction between the components of Ni-based MDESs than in Co-based MDESS, which is consistent with the result of the FTIR experiment. This trend is compatible with the Mark-Houwink equation commonly used to describe the viscosity behavior of polymers.45 The trend of the viscosity-temperature profile of these MDESs could be explained by the Hole Theory, which describes the influencing factors of the viscosity of ILs as well as DESs.44 When heating the MDESS, the increased intramolecular energy speeds up the molecular motion and then the formed large hole will permit molecules to pass through each other easily, thereby decreasing the viscosity. In general, the viscosity values of MDESs are similar to those of ILs (50 to 10000 mP s at 25 °C).

Thus, the conductivity is necessary information for considering the application of MDESs. In general, the conductivity values increase following the increase in temperature because the kinetic energy from heat promotes the frequent collisions between molecules, thereby weakening the intermolecular forces of DES.44 The conductivity values of MDESs were experimentally determined at different temperatures which are 25, 35, 45, 55, 65 and 75 °C, respectively. At 25 °C, the con- ductivity values range from 209 to 9530 µS cm⁻¹. It is known that the conductivity of a DES is highly affected by its viscosity and ion concentration. It was reported that a viscous DES always gives a lower conductivity.⁴⁶ As hypothesized, MDES2 with the highest viscosity has the lowest conductivity value. pH and surface tension pH is an important physical property and it is basic for DESs to apply in catalysis, metal treatment, gas absorption and biomass dissolution. Thus, the pH values of these MDESs were measured at room temperature and the results are recorded in Table 2. From the table, it can be seen that the pH values range from 0.4 to 3.9, demonstrating that all MDESs behave with an acidic characteristic. Among them, the LA-based MDESs exhibit a stronger acidity than the others which might be due to the existence of a carboxylic acid group. Moreover, when using the same HBD, the MDESs have similar pH values, which resembles the same system with different HBD content as well (see Table S2, ESI†). Thus, the HBD components might have an effect on the pH behavior of MDESs which is consistent with a previous report.53

Surface tension is an energy which actually requires an increase in the surface area of a liquid by a unit of area. It can be used to understand the intermolecular forces between molecules in the mixture.⁵⁴ It is also an essential physical factor for industrial processes and chemical applications. In this study, we measured the surface tension of all MDESS at 25 °C. As is shown in Table 2, the surface tension values are located between 35.0 and 89.9 mN m⁻¹. On account of the higher viscosity, MDES2 has no surface tension data to record. When using the same HBD components, the Ni-based MDESS always have higher surface tension values than Co-based MDESS. This might be owing to the stronger H-bonding inter- action between HBD and NiCl₂·6H₂O than CoCl₂·6H₂O. The results indicate that HBA is an influencing factor to surface tension. For the MDESs with the same HBA, the surface tension order follows amide-based MDESS > alcohol-based MDESS > carboxylic acid-based MDESs in this work. Moreover, the MDESs have similar surface tension values to common DESS at 25 °C, such as ChCl:EG (49.4 mN m⁻¹), ChCl:LA (44.4 mN m⁻¹), FeCl₃·6H₂O:EG (57.0 mN m⁻¹) and so on.⁵⁵ And the majority of typical ILs have surface tension values between 40 and 50 mN m⁻¹.⁵⁶ Thus, the MDESs are comparable to common DESS and ILs.

Thus, the pH values of these MDESs were measured at room temperature and the results are recorded in Table 2. From the table, it can be seen that the pH values range from 0.4 to 3.9, demonstrating that all MDESs behave with an acidic characteristic. It can be used to understand the intermolecular forces between molecules in the mixture.⁵⁴ It is also an essential physical factor for industrial processes and chemical applications. In this study, we measured the surface tension of all MDESS at 25 °C. As is shown in Table 2, the surface tension values are located between 35.0 and 89.9 mN m⁻¹. On account of the higher viscosity, MDES2 has no surface tension data to record. When using the same HBD components, the Ni-based MDESS always have higher surface tension values than Co-based MDESS.
